newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. June CPI up 0.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. June CPI up 0.1 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the June Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent compared to a 0.1-percent increase in May. Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2-percent rise in CPI, and the same increase minus volatile food and energy items.

CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH & CO INC: "It sounds like the cast of characters that caused the number to be lower turned out to be the case with apparel prices being lower, furniture prices being lower ...
"I think what this is telling us is that there's almost a complete lack of inflationary pressures in the economy," added Katz, who was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

CARY LEAHEY, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, HIGH FREQUENCY ECONOMICS: "People were expecting a good number and we got a great number. That kind of factoid -- the smallest six-month increase in 11 years since 1986 -- is the kind of news the market jumps on. Numbers like this reduce the chances of the (Federal Reserve) moving in August from probably 20 percent to down to five to 10 percent ... getting closer to zero."
JAMES GLASSMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "What is going on is that import prices have been falling since last year related to all this capacity built in Asia.
"We're benefitting from this disinflation abroad. The dollar rising further this year is adding fuel to that.

"The decline in import prices relative to U.S. inflation is easily enough to hold the core inflation rate down by 1/2 to one full point. There'e every reason to think this year's core rate of inflation will be off a little bit from last year."
MORTON SWINSKY, PRESIDENT AND CEO, FUJI SECURITIES INC: "This is very positive for the bond market. I'm of the opinion that we're headed to lower yields by year end, there's no doubt about it."
Swinsky said he "absolutely" expected the tame inflation scenario to continue.

"The numbers continue to fall right in line. We're looking as an analogy to the period of time that took interest rates down in the '60s," and bond yields of around 6.00-percent by year-end, he added.
PETER D'ANTONIO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITICORP GLOBAL FINANCE: "It's as good as it gets. Apparel and transportation both fell. That gave us the lower-than-expected reading.

"Trends haven't changed much. If anything, it still seems to be sliding a little bit. On a year-to-year basis, the core rate is at 2.4 percent. And last year the core CPI rose 2.6 percent. The first half of this year, the core CPI has been the lowest for a half-year in 32 years. It's been low for a long time and it's easing a little further.

"The Fed keeps looking for tight labor markets to give us higher inflation and they're puzzled why they're not getting it. They ought to ask themselves why they're getting lower inflation. Perhaps the labor markets are not as tight as they think, notwithstanding the employment rate. We look for the core CPI to end the year around 2.5 percent," he added.
